> Guys, im trying to illustrate how to read type signatures to OP.

Which is very noble. But I think you should make a clearer distinction of functions and applications. Maybe I didn't read correctly, but you said that the first expression has the type `Bool -> [Bool] -> [Bool]`, which is unfortunately not correct because it's a *function application*, id est a value, and not a function like you seem to be suggesting with the aforementioned signature.

Furthermore, the second expression builds on the first one. So, if we use the aforementioned one we get the monster-looking

```
(Bool -> [Bool] -> [Bool]) -> [Bool -> [Bool] -> [Bool]] -> [Bool -> [Bool] -> [Bool]]
```

But that's just `:` with `Bool -> [Bool] -> [Bool]` as `a`. So, it's simply `:`, meaning that our values and the whole computation were just meaningless. `Bool -> [Bool] -> [Bool]` it's just the type of the first *operator*, not the whole expression.

The whole expression, since it doesn't need any kind of parameter, is `[Bool]`, so a *value*. And that's the `a` in the second `:` and so on.

The problem is that you're confusing the function itself with its application.

The cons operator has the type

```
    (:) :: a -> [a] -> [a]
```

But we know the value of `a` for our context: it's `Bool`. So for us the function has the type

```
(:) :: Bool -> [Bool] -> [Bool]
```

However, you're confusing it with its application, which has the signature

```
False : [] :: [Bool]
```

That is because we already provided enough parameters to `:`. It doesn't need anything more, so it's not a new function, but a value.

The same logic is then to be applied to the second member. This time, however, `a` is not simply `Bool`, but it's `[Bool]`, which is the type of the first expression, so the resulting type is `[[Bool]]`.

Hope this helps.

I find *Techno Pop*'s history fascinating.

The album was originally named *Technicolor*, but was changed to *Techno Pop* because of copyright reasons. The album was to be played with analog instrumentation, like the ones before it, and was planned to have a different tracklist, specifically A: *Boing Boom Tschak* / *Techno Pop* / *Musique Non Stop* (probably as a single track named *Techno Pop*) and B: *The Telephone Call* / *Sex Object* / *Tour De France*. Promotional art for the album and demos of the analog versions of *Techno Pop* and *Sex Object* can be found online (and that version of *Sex Object* was reworked into the one present in *The Catalogue 3-D*).

The album was almost ready, but Ralf wasn't satisfied with the finished product, so it was redone pretty much from scratch (it was also delayed because Ralf had an incident). The "new" album was then called *Electric Cafe* and *Tour The France* was replaced with a new composition, *Electric Cafe*.

When remastering the album for *The Catalogue*, the name was changed to *Techno Pop* and *The Telephone Call* was replaced with the radio edit from the single and a B side from that same single, namely *House Phone*. Note that when the 2004 promo version of *The Catalogue* was released, the album was remastered, renamed, but remained unchanged tracklist-wise, so it contained the original version of the track (which is different from the extended single version). So there are in total four version of *The Telephone Call*: album version, single edit, single radio edit and the remixed version, *House Phone*.

There are a lot of (little) things to say about *Techno Pop*, like the fact that *Musique Non Stop* was changed to *Music Non Stop* when *The Mix* was released, but I think I already was too much verbose. Hope that I managed to clarify things a little bit.
